title: Asia in the Sunset Empires Era
summary: The Kuei-jin in nineteenth-century Asia, when mortal history outran the undead.

claims.text: In this era mortal events, not the Kuei-jin, the Kin-jin or the hengeyokai, drive the great changes sweeping Asia.
The Kuei-jin are no longer dominant, though they have not yet grasped it; this humbling is the hardest they have known since Wan Xian fell.
Cainites lived in Asia far longer than most ancestors admit, and existed there only because the Kuei-jin let them.

title: Kin-jin in the Treaty Ports
summary: Western vampires riding colonial power into Asia.

claims.text: Western vampires survive this period more easily because they have learned to hide inside whatever society rules the day.
At first the Kuei-jin hold back from striking the Western undead, fearing the political cost.
Many Cathayans let Kin-jin settle in their cities, used them for private schemes and even trusted them as go-betweens with the outside world.
In many Chinese cities a Kin-jin prince holds the foreign quarter, often under the cover of European treaty rights.
Some of the Western vampires in Shanghai belong to the Hellfire Clubs, drawn to the East by its occult mysteries.

title: The Fall of the Flame Court
summary: How the southern court broke under the Opium Wars.

claims.text: Seers say the Flame Court stands for the south, for greater yang, upheaval and change.
As war with Britain loomed, the court fell into quarrels and covert feuds, as many wu schemed separately to drive the British out.
In the end the court was declared collapsed, a verdict that spread to the other August Courts.
Kin-jin, and the Tremere above all, saw a chance to set up new domains along the southern coast.

title: The Flesh Court of Shanghai
summary: The most open of the Quincunx courts toward foreigners.

claims.text: The Flesh Court Wan Kuei are the most progressive in the Quincunx, and they understand the Western mind better than any other court.
The Quincunx already viewed the Flesh Court with suspicion for its mild stance on heretical Dharmas.
The court is openly curious about and tolerant of foreigners, and no other region of China is as wealthy.
When the Taiping took Nanjing, rival courts spent nearly twenty years in shadow wars for indirect control of the city.
